To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
two extraordinarily long bacterial symbionts attached to nematodes reproduce by symmetric division and that size is not a limiting factor for cell division in bacteria.
two extraordinarily long bacterial symbionts reproduce by constriction of a single Fts Z ring and that the size of the cells is independent of their length.
two extraordinarily long bacteria divide in a size-independent manner and that this is achieved through the formation of a single Fts Z ring at midcell.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the reproduction of two extraordinarily long cells.
the ultrastructure, morphology and cell biology of bacteria that live in symbiosis with nematodes.
the ultrastructure, morphology and cell division of two long bacteria that are associated with marine nematodes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cell size of bacteria is limited by the cell wall synthesis, not by cell division.
size is not an intrinsic limitation to symmetric division in bacteria.
the size of a bacterial cell is irrelevant in determining its mode of reproduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
size-independent division in extraordinarily long bacteria is possible.
size-independent symmetric division in extremely long cells is not an exception, but rather the rule.
the bacteria in the nematodes E. fertilis and E. dianeae are the longest unicellular organisms known to divide symmetrically.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cell size is not a limiting factor in symmetric cell division, at least in the case of the two symbionts described here.
size is not a limiting factor for cell division and that the mechanisms that control the localization of both the DNA and the septal ring in bacteria are yet to be discovered.
the cell cycle can be uncoupled from cell size.
